Every angle question on the SAT comes down to three ideas: one eighty, ninety, and equal. Learn when to use each one, and you can solve them all.
Start with a straight line. Think of a door that swings all the way open, flat against the wall. That full swing is one hundred eighty degrees.
Put a ray anywhere on the line, and it splits that one eighty into two angles. Together they always make one eighty. If one is one thirty, the other is fifty.
Now cross two lines, like a pair of scissors. Open the blades wider, and both opposite angles grow together.
Angles across from each other are called vertical angles, and they are always equal. Angles side by side sit on a straight line, so they add to one eighty.
Next, triangles. Tear the three corners off any triangle and set them side by side.
They fit together into a straight line. So the three angles of every triangle add up to one hundred eighty degrees.
In a right triangle, the square corner already uses ninety. That leaves ninety for the other two angles.
Now picture railroad tracks: two parallel lines, cut by a road that crosses them. That road is called a transversal.
Slide the top crossing down onto the bottom one. It lands exactly on top. Every angle at one crossing repeats at the other.
So there are only two sizes. All the small, acute angles are equal. All the big, obtuse angles are equal. And small plus big makes one eighty.
Let's try an SAT style question. Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One angle is sixty five degrees. What is the obtuse angle?
Step one. Mark what you know. The sixty five degree angle is acute.
Step two. The obtuse angle is the big one, and small plus big is one eighty.
Step three. One eighty minus sixty five is one fifteen. The obtuse angle is one hundred fifteen degrees.
Trap alert. Sixty five is also an answer choice. But an obtuse angle is bigger than ninety, so it can't be sixty five.
One more. A triangle has angles of fifty and sixty degrees. What is the third angle?
Fifty plus sixty is one ten. One eighty minus one ten is seventy. The third angle is seventy degrees.
Don't stop at one ten. That's only the two angles added together. Always subtract from one eighty.
Your turn. Pause the video. A right triangle has a thirty five degree angle. What is the other acute angle?
The right angle uses ninety, so the other two share ninety. Ninety minus thirty five is fifty five. If you got one forty five, you subtracted from one eighty and forgot the right angle.
Remember three things. A straight line and a triangle are both one eighty. Vertical angles are equal. Parallel lines repeat the same two angles. Great work.
